note: Korean has no verb 'to have' for possession in everyday speech. 'I have time' is 시간이 있어요 — 'time exists (for me).' The owner is just understood.
맛 (taste) + 있다 (exists). Its opposite, 맛없어요, is literally 'taste doesn't exist' = it tastes bad. The 'exists' pattern builds many words.
Koreans say 'our' for things tied to a shared group — family, home, country, company — even when speaking only for themselves. Saying 내 엄마 ('my mom') sounds oddly possessive.
The body part is the subject: 배 (stomach/belly) + 고프다. No 'I' needed — context supplies it. Same family: 배불러요 ('stomach is full') = I'm full.
Qualities are often expressed through body parts: a good head = intelligence. Its cousin 눈이 높다 ('eyes are high') means having picky standards.
A warm everyday greeting, historically rooted in times when a full meal wasn't guaranteed. Nobody is actually asking about your meal — answer 네 (yes) and greet back.
Said before a meal to the cook or host — gratitude packaged as a promise. Its bookend, 잘 먹었습니다 ('I ate well'), is said after finishing.

real: good work today / thanks for your effort
note: The standard sign-off with coworkers, staff, or anyone who did work — acknowledging effort itself rather than results. English has no everyday equivalent.

real: you can do it! / good luck!
note: Borrowed from English 'fighting' but repurposed as pure encouragement — before exams, interviews, games. Nothing combative about it.

real: this hits the spot (even about hot soup!)
note: Famously said while eating scalding-hot soup or sitting in a hot bath. It describes the refreshed, unblocked feeling — not the temperature.
Between neighbors and acquaintances this is often just a greeting, not an interrogation. A vague answer like 그냥요 ('just...') is completely fine.

real: the art of reading a room
note: The skill of sensing others' moods and the unspoken situation. You can have fast 눈치, lack it (눈치 없다), or 'see 눈치' (눈치를 보다) — anxiously gauging others' reactions.

real: deep attachment that grows over time
note: The bond that accumulates between people who share time — friends, family, even a grumpy neighbor. You can have 정 for someone you don't especially like. It explains a lot of Korean social life.
The specific feeling of a blocked chest: slow wifi, a friend who won't take advice, a stuck situation, an airless room. Physical and emotional at once — English needs a whole sentence for it.
The soft regret when something good ends too soon or almost worked out — leaving a great trip, losing narrowly, a friend moving away. Not sad exactly; wistful.
The universal answer to 'why?' when there is no why. 왜 왔어요? (Why'd you come?) — 그냥. It deflects gently without being rude. Massively common in real speech.
도 doesn't stack on the particles you know — it replaces them. 음악을도 is wrong; the single 도 carries both the 'object' job and the 'also' job at once.

real: headed there vs. doing something there
note: 에 points at a destination (or where something exists); 에서 marks where an action happens. 학교에 가요 — go TO school. 학교에서 공부해요 — study AT school. Mixing them is the classic learner tell.
One particle, two English jobs. Between nouns it's 'and': 우유하고 빵 (milk and bread). After a noun, before the action, it's 'with': 친구하고 봤어요 (watched it with a friend). Context decides.
The standard greeting after time apart — the past tense of 지내다 (to spend time / get along). Answer by bouncing it back: 네, 잘 지냈어요.

English 'don't' blurs what Korean splits: 안 is a decision, 못 is inability or circumstance. 술 안 마셔요 — I choose not to drink. 술 못 마셔요 — I can't (health, driving, tolerance). Koreans hear the difference instantly.

real: I want vs. he/she seems to want
note: Korean grammar marks WHOSE desire it is. -고 싶어요 is for your own (or your listener's) wants; describing a third person's takes -고 싶어해요 — you can only report the wanting they display, not feel it for them.

치킨 + 맥주 squashed into one word — a whole social institution: after-work gatherings, summer river picnics, watching the game. Korean loves these portmanteaus; learn the parts and you can often decode the whole.
